editorial.headline: Business & Employer Organisations: Open Nationally, Address-Sensitive in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A national business or employer organisation may be fully foreign-owned, while Bali requires risk classification and address-level verification.
editorial.body:
This activity is the institutional work of business and employer organisations: bodies formed to advance the development and welfare of member enterprises in a particular trade, commerce, agriculture, economic-growth agenda or geographic area. It also embraces federations of associations, chambers of commerce and similar organisations, as well as the practical work through which business interests are informed, represented before government institutions, communicated publicly and carried into labour negotiations. The focus is collective representation of enterprise interests, rather than the operation of an individual commercial business.

The record does not assign this activity to any stated business scale. That absence matters: it leaves the editorial point where it belongs, on the nature of the organisation and the investment position recorded for it, rather than implying a size threshold that has not been supplied. Organisations registering under this activity are those whose members gather around business, trade, agricultural, economic or place-based interests, and whose work may include association-building, chamber-style representation, public relations, information-sharing and employment negotiations.

Nationally, the position is clear. The activity is marked **TERBUKA**, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of **100%**. Put simply, the record allows full foreign ownership nationwide. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. That national openness is the central fact for a foreign investor considering this organisational form: there is no recorded foreign-equity cap below full ownership.

Bali adds a more location-specific reading, without reversing the national result. Its status is **OK_or_HIGHER_RISK** and the record describes the activity as medium-high or high risk, so it is not blocked by the provincial moratorium. The moratorium blocks PMA registration for all low and medium-low risk KBLI activities across the province on a permanent, island-wide basis; this activity is recorded outside that blocked risk range. Even so, the record expressly calls for verification by address. For a Bali registration, the honest conclusion is therefore neither a blanket prohibition nor an automatic clearance: the activity is not moratorium-blocked, but its position should be confirmed for the proposed address.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally, this activity permits full foreign ownership; in Bali, it is not moratorium-blocked but still requires address-level verification.
